statement: Do not reduce weekly volume, quality-session count or progression rate based on age alone; adjust only from observed tolerance, soreness, performance trend and injury signals. Reduced training volume and intensity is itself a major mediator of the age-related decline.

Keep the same minimum gap between hard sessions for masters as for younger runners; one controlled study found no age difference in physical recovery (strength, sprint, time trial, CK) within 48 h of a repeated-interval session. The 48 h value is an engine convention.
appliesTo: Trained masters (about 50-60 y studied, cyclists); extrapolated to runners

statement: For masters, collect a perceived-recovery rating (soreness, fatigue, motivation) after hard sessions; if ratings remain poor at about 48 h, defer the next quality session or convert it to easy aerobic running. The rating threshold is not given by the evidence: use a conservative default (for example soreness or fatigue worse than the runner's own recent median).

The age-related recovery-demand multiplier on rest between hard sessions defaults to 1.0; allow it to rise only from the runner's own data, capped at a modest value. The cap is a conservative engineering default, not an evidence-derived number.

For multi-year goal-time projection (not within-block prescription), keep speed targets flat to age 35, then apply a decline defaulting to about 0.7% per year (band 0.5-1.0%) from 35 to 70, with the slope a user-fittable parameter. Decline accelerates with age, so avoid a single constant for all decades; fit to the runner's own history when more than 2 years of data exist.
appliesTo: Recreational and competitive road runners, both sexes

statement: After age 70 multiply the age-decline slope by 1.4-1.7 (men 1.7, women 1.4 in track and field data); use 1.5 as a sex-neutral default.

Condition the decline slope on training consistency: use the optimistic rate (about 0.67% per year) only for runners with consistent year-round training; for inconsistent or detrained runners use a higher slope (up to about 1.0% per year, higher for long breaks). The consistency threshold is not defined by the evidence; a default is more than 80% of planned weeks completed (engineering default, grade D).

When no measured maximum exists, seed HRmax with 208 - 0.7 x age (not 220 - age) and display a +/-10 bpm uncertainty; 211 - 0.64 x age is a sensitivity alternative (about 6-7 bpm higher at ages 60-70). Do not adjust by sex or training status.

Replace the age-based HRmax prior with an observed maximum from reliable hard efforts (artefact-filtered, ideally chest-strap) using a rolling window rather than an all-time maximum, and expect observed HRmax to fall about 5-7 bpm per decade regardless of training.

Keep at least one quality session (threshold or interval) per week in build phases for masters when recovery signals allow; intensity appears more important than total minutes for maintaining VO2peak at higher ages (association, self-reported activity).
appliesTo: Runners 40+ in build phases, if tolerated

statement: Include resistance training for masters runners to preserve lean mass (HRmax decline is not trainable, lean mass partly is); the 1-2 sessions per week figure is an engine default, not a measured dose.

Apply a soft cap on run days per week with at least one rest or cross-training day for 40+. Higher weekly frequency raised injury risk in both age groups, but the paper gives no threshold, so 6 days is a conservative default, not an evidence-derived value.

For runners 40+, include calf, Achilles and hamstring strengthening and progress hills and speedwork gradually, since these soft-tissue sites were more often injured in masters; treat the extra risk as exposure-related and modest, not as a reason for an age-specific load rule.

Present WMA-style age-graded scores only as a labelled comparison to elite-derived standards, never as the basis for setting targets or goal realism; use the runner's own longitudinal trend. No validation of the WMA factor tables was found in this corpus, and record-list curves appear to understate decline for slower runners.
appliesTo: All runners, especially recreational and slower masters

statement: For 100 km to 100-mile goals, apply no age-related target decline before about age 50 (best 100 km times observed at 30-49 men, 30-54 women; Western States fastest men comparable at 30-39 and 40-49), then use the general decline curve. Evidence is cross-sectional race data; low confidence.
